extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and educated readers of Nature interested in scientific method and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging scientific reasoning, models, and inferences: how well explanations translate observations into intellectual representations, the role of assumptions and expert judgment, and the standards for verification and causal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to known or ascertainable facts and predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific conception is justified either by its conformity to known or ascertainable facts (e.g., Kepler’s determination of Mars’ orbit), by the fulfilment of the predictions it sanctions (e.g., eclipses, occultations), or by the discovery of previously unrecognised phenomena predicted by it (e.g., perturbations leading to discovery of a planet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples (Kepler, Newton, discovery of Uranus’ perturbing planet) as standards: models should match observed facts and make testable predictions whose fulfilment strengthens the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of phenomena into intellectual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: All scientific reasoning involves translating actual phenomena into intellectual representations or models; even the 'exact' sciences proceed by such representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise models as mental constructions; evaluate whether the representation is appropriate for the data and whether its conceptual apparatus is coherent and necessary for the inference made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit recognition and evaluation of underlying assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many scientific inferences rest on assumptions (e.g., that a spectral line seen in the Sun means hydrogen as in terrestrial flames, or assumptions about probable distances of perturbing planets); such assumptions may have high probability but are not demonstrative certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make assumptions explicit, assess their probability, and seek independent verification (example: Crookes’ Thallium—spectral line later matched by discovery of a new metal). Distinguish between highly probable premises and those requiring further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ad hoc hypotheses that merely 'save appearances'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations that add contrivances solely to match observations (like Ptolemaic 'Centric and Excentric, Cycle and Epicycle, Orb in Orb') are to be distrusted unless they correspond to real causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations that posit real, testable causes rather than adding mechanisms solely to fit data; be skeptical of hypotheses introduced only to preserve an existing scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification by fulfilment of predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The fulfilment of predictions (e.g., an eclipse occurring at a specified future time) serves as important evidence for the correctness of the explanatory scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successful predictions as strong supporting evidence, but not as sole proof of the correctness of underlying reasoning (see related caution about accidental correctness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of expert judgment and trained 'common sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scientific interpretations are matters of judgment whose value depends on the qualifications of the individual (e.g., geology depends heavily on specially-trained 'common sense').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether interpretations rely on suitably trained expertise; recognise that some domains require domain-specific cultivated judgment that ordinary intuition may not supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs gain trustworthiness when multiple independent experiences or lines of reasoning converge upon the same conclusion (the 'convergence of all our lines of thought' gives weight to common-sense conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek corroboration across different methods, datasets, or perspectives; accumulation of concordant observations increases confidence (example: flint implements becoming 'self-evident' through accumulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and validation of instruments through known objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments (telescope, microscope, spectroscope) must be validated by applying them to known objects so that their revelations can be interpreted with confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test instruments on familiar cases to learn to distinguish true from false signals; treat instrument output as requiring mental judgment grounded in prior experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and cross‑coordination of multiple sensory/data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate perception and interpretation often require coordination (e.g., visual and tactile senses must be co-ordinated by experience); single data streams are liable to misinterpretation without cross-validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine independent types of data (senses, instruments, methods) and validate interpretations by cross-checking between them (example: sight alone vs sight+touch for object recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between efficient cause (force) and material conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Good causal analysis distinguishes the dynamical power (the efficient cause or 'Force') from the material conditions or circumstances under which it acts (e.g., the pulling handle transmits force from a steam engine; ignition liberates stored chemical energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning causes, identify the power that does the work separately from the conditions that enable or modify its action; avoid conflating immediately preceding events with the true efficient cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of foundational axioms and primary beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some elements of scientific reasoning rest on assumed axioms or 'primary beliefs' (e.g., axioms of geometry, Uniformity of Nature) which are accepted because they are self-evident or inherited, not demonstrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly acknowledge foundational assumptions, understand their role, and avoid treating them as empirically proven; consider their provenance (intuition, culture, previous generations' experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate assignment of probabilistic confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many inferences should be judged in terms of probability rather than demonstrative certainty; reasoning may be justified by a sufficiently high probability even if not absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between high-probability conclusions and certainties; state degrees of confidence and pursue further evidence when the assumption is of low security (example: Helium attribution vs hydrogen line identification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about 'happy accidents' and retrospective justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct outcome may have arisen from accidental or erroneous reasoning (Kepler's 'series of happy accidents'); success does not necessarily validate the original mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the causal chain of discovery; do not retroactively ascribe reliability to methods merely because their conclusions happened to be correct—seek reproducible rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for dynamical (force-based) explanations over mere phenomenological generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: A dynamical conception that explains phenomena in terms of forces and mechanisms (Newton) is of higher value than mere generalisation of observed facts without causal account (Kepler’s laws as pure generalisations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor explanatory frameworks that supply underlying mechanisms and causal principles rather than those that only summarize regularities; evaluate whether a model provides dynamical understanding, not just description.
